title: Human Expert Evaluation of Agentic AI for EO, form F19
description:
Thank you for helping us evaluate the performance of different LLMs in Agentic AI frameworks for EO!

WHAT THIS IS
We built a benchmark to test the performance of different LLMs in agentic settings. This evaluation form is to compare the answers given by these LLMs when answering a question using different tools related to the agentic framework that we built - including different EO endpoints (Copernicus/Sentinel, Landsat), ERA5 climate data, EO Dashboard narratives, ESA science strategy documents, GIS analysis and scientific literature search.

You will be given 8 questions, and for each question you see every anonymous answer that assistant actually produced for it -- usually several, occasionally just one if only one assistant answered that particular question.

WHAT YOU DO
(About 49 minutes for this form -- your progress is saved in this browser, so it's fine to do this over more than one sitting.) The form will guide you through it, but for every question you will
1. Rate how relevant and realistic the question is for EO users.
2. Score the accuracy of each answer shown.
3. If there's more than one answer, rank them all from best to worst (skip this step when only one answer is shown -- there's nothing to compare it to).

HOW TO JUDGE ACCURACY
Judge scientific and domain correctness, and whether the answer addresses every part of the question. A minority of answers (marked "▣ image" next to the answer letter) include the actual image the assistant looked at -- check the description against it directly. For every other answer you cannot open the files or images it says it produced: treat claims that you find implausible or unsupported as errors. Do not reward length or formatting. If you cannot judge a question, say so in the comment field and give your best estimate.

Answers were produced automatically and may contain errors. Local file paths were removed from the answers. Long answers are collapsed by default — click an answer to expand it.

PRIVACY
Your name is recorded so we can follow up if needed, and is not shown to other experts. Responses are used only for the research evaluation of this benchmark and are reported in aggregate. Participation is voluntary; you can stop at any time by closing the page.

profile_fields.title: Name
profile_fields.help: So we know who a response came from. Not shown to other experts.

profile_fields.title: How would you rate your Earth Observation expertise?
Which areas are you experienced in?
choices: Climate and atmospheric data (ERA5, trace gases)
EO science strategy and scientific literature

profile_fields.title: Consent
choices: I agree that my responses are used for the research evaluation of this benchmark.

relevance.title: How relevant and realistic is this question for EO users (researchers, analysts, practitioners)?
relevance.help: 1 = not relevant or unrealistic; 3 = plausible but marginal or somewhat artificial; 5 = highly relevant and realistic.

accuracy.title: Accuracy: how correct and complete is each answer?
accuracy.help: 1 = incorrect or unusable; 2 = mostly incorrect or major omissions; 3 = partially correct or incomplete; 4 = mostly correct, minor issues; 5 = correct and complete. Equal scores are allowed.

ranking.title: Ranking: order all answers from best to worst.
ranking.help: Drag, or use the arrows, to put the best answer at the top and the worst at the bottom. Ties are not allowed.

familiarity.title: How familiar are you with the topic of this question?

comment.title: Comment (optional)
comment.help: For example: an error you spotted, why a question is not relevant, or that you could not judge it.

items.question: Download a Sentinel-1 GRD SAR image of the Po Delta, northern Italy for October 2023 to assess wetland extent and soil moisture. Describe the main backscatter patterns visible in the image and identify areas likely associated with wetlands or open water.

answers.text:
Based on the Sentinel-1 GRD SAR image of the Po Delta region (northern Italy, October 2023), the following observations can be made regarding backscatter patterns and wetland/ open water identification:

Backscatter Patterns:
• High Backscatter (Bright Areas - Orange/Yellow): These areas correspond to land surfaces with higher reflectivity, such as urbanized zones, dense vegetation, or dry soil. The bright orange patches indicate relatively dry or structured surfaces.
• Low Backscatter (Dark Areas - Blue/Purple): These areas represent surfaces with low reflectivity, such as open water, wetlands, or very smooth surfaces. The dominant blue/purple regions along the coastline and inland suggest these are likely wetlands or open water bodies.

Wetland and Open Water Identification:
• Coastal and Inland Wetlands: The large, contiguous dark blue areas along the coastline and extending inland are highly indicative of wetlands or open water. These areas appear as low backscatter zones, which is typical for water bodies in SAR imagery.
• River Channels and Estuaries: The dark blue patches along the river systems and estuaries further support the presence of water bodies, as these areas show low backscatter due to the smooth, reflective surface of water.
• Potential Wetland Zones: The irregularly shaped dark patches inland, particularly near the river mouths, are likely wetland areas. These areas may be influenced by seasonal flooding or tidal effects, which are common in the Po Delta region.

Conclusion:
The image clearly shows a contrast between high backscatter (dry land) and low backscatter (wetlands/open water). The dominant blue/purple areas, especially along the coastline and river systems, are most likely wetlands or open water, consistent with the known hydrological characteristics of the Po Delta region. This analysis supports the use of SAR imagery for assessing wetland extent and soil moisture in this area.

The Sentinel-1 GRD SAR image of the Po Delta, northern Italy, for October 2023, displays distinct backscatter patterns that are useful for assessing wetland extent and soil moisture. The image uses a pseudo-RGB composite (VV, VH, VV/VH ratio) which enhances the contrast between different surface types.

Main Backscatter Patterns:
1. High Backscatter (Bright Areas - White/Orange): These areas typically correspond to dry, hard surfaces such as urban areas, roads, and bare soil. The bright orange and white patches indicate surfaces with high radar reflectivity, likely due to their roughness or low moisture content.

2. Medium Backscatter (Pink/Magenta): These areas often represent semi-urban or agricultural land with moderate moisture content or vegetation cover. The pink and magenta tones suggest a mix of surface types, possibly including wet fields or areas with sparse vegetation.

3. Low Backscatter (Dark Blue/Black): These areas are indicative of open water or wetlands. The dark blue and black regions, especially along the riverbanks and coastal zones, show very low radar reflectivity, which is characteristic of water surfaces that absorb most of the radar signal.

Areas Likely Associated with Wetlands or Open Water:
• Coastal and Riverine Zones: The dark blue/black areas along the coastline and river channels are most likely open water or wetlands. These areas appear as elongated, contiguous patches, suggesting they are part of the delta’s natural water systems.

• Inland Wetlands: Some dark patches inland, particularly near the riverbanks and in low-lying areas, may represent wetlands. These areas are likely to have high moisture content, which reduces radar backscatter.

• Delta Channels: The river channels and their tributaries appear as dark blue/black lines, indicating they are filled with water. These channels are part of the delta’s hydrological system and are likely to be associated with wetlands.

Conclusion:
The image clearly shows a contrast between dry, high-backscatter areas (urban, agricultural) and low-backscatter areas (water, wetlands). The dark blue/black regions, especially along the riverbanks and coastal zones, are most likely open water or wetlands. This visual analysis supports the assessment of wetland extent and soil moisture in the Po Delta region.

However, the image data appears to be insufficient for direct visualization or analysis, as it is a specialized SAR dataset with specific backscatter values (VV and VH polarizations) rather than a standard RGB image.

In SAR imagery, backscatter patterns are interpreted as follows:
• High backscatter (bright areas): Typically indicate surfaces with rough textures or high reflectivity, such as urban areas, dry soil, or vegetation with dense structure.
• Low backscatter (dark areas): Usually correspond to smooth or wet surfaces, such as open water, flooded areas, or bare soil with low reflectivity.

For the Po Delta region, areas likely associated with wetlands or open water would appear as dark regions in the SAR image due to their smooth surface and low backscatter. These areas may be contrasted with brighter regions representing land cover such as vegetation, urban areas, or dry soil.

To accurately assess wetland extent and soil moisture, quantitative analysis using the SAR data (e.g., gamma0 values) is required, which is beyond the scope of visual interpretation. The GeoTIFF file can be processed with specialized software (e.g., SNAP, QGIS, or Python libraries like rasterio) to extract quantitative metrics for wetland mapping and soil moisture estimation.

If you need further assistance with processing or interpreting the SAR data, please let me know!

Based on the Sentinel-1 GRD SAR image of the Po Delta, northern Italy, acquired in October 2023, the following observations can be made regarding backscatter patterns and wetland/soil moisture extent:

Backscatter Patterns:
• High Backscatter (Bright Areas - Orange/Pink): These areas correspond to dry, hard surfaces such as agricultural fields, urban areas, or compacted soil. The high backscatter is due to strong radar reflection from these surfaces.
• Low Backscatter (Dark Areas - Blue/Black): These areas indicate surfaces with low radar reflectivity, such as open water, wetlands, or very moist soil. The radar signal is absorbed or scattered minimally in these regions.

Wetland and Open Water Identification:
• Blue/Black Regions: The prominent blue and black areas, especially along the coastline and inland, are likely associated with wetlands or open water bodies. These areas show minimal backscatter, which is characteristic of water surfaces that absorb radar energy.
• Networked Blue Areas: The interconnected blue patches suggest a network of channels, marshes, or flooded areas typical of the Po Delta’s wetland system.
• Coastal Zones: The extensive blue areas along the coastline indicate significant wetland or open water coverage, which is consistent with the delta’s natural hydrology.

Conclusion:
The image clearly highlights the spatial extent of wetlands and open water in the Po Delta region. The low backscatter areas (blue/black) are strong indicators of water presence, while the high backscatter areas (orange/pink) represent dry or urbanized land. This analysis supports the assessment of wetland extent and soil moisture conditions in the region for October 2023.

items.question: Identify the ESA Earth Observation Science Strategy research priorities related to sea-level rise, then search arXiv for recent papers addressing those topics. Summarize how the recent research supports or expands on the identified ESA priorities.

answers.text:
Here are the key ESA Earth Observation Science Strategy research priorities related to sea-level rise, along with recent papers (last 2-3 years) that align with these priorities, and a summary of how the research supports or expands on the identified ESA priorities:

1. Ice Mass Balance and Cryosphere Dynamics
ESA EO Science Strategy Priority:
• Science Question (SQ-20): What are the drivers of ice-sheet and glacier mass balance and snow cover change, and what are the impacts of such changes in the Earth system?
  • Addresses ScienceTheme ST-I (Water Cycle) and ST-III (Energy Fluxes).
  • Informs Treaty PARIS (Art 4 Mitigation; Art 7/8 Adaptation and Loss/Damage).
  • Linked to Tipping Points: Ice Sheets (TP-01), Sea Ice (TP-02), Glaciers (TP-03), and Permafrost (TP-04).
  • Knowledge Advancement Objectives (KAOs):
    • KAO-SQ20-20A: Improve quantitative estimation of cryosphere components (e.g., ice sheet mass balance, glacier area/volume).
    • KAO-SQ20-20B: Strengthen understanding of regional ice mass loss patterns.

Recent Papers (2021–2024):
• Slater et al. (2020) – Ice-sheet losses track high-end sea-level rise projections. Nature Climate Change, 10, 879–881.
  • Highlights the alignment of observed ice-sheet losses with high-end sea-level rise projections.
  • DOI: 10.1038/s41558-020-0893-y (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41558-020-0893-y)

• Davison et al. (2023b) – Sea level rise from West Antarctic mass loss significantly modified by large snowfall anomalies. Nature Communications, 14, 1–10.
  • Demonstrates how snowfall variability in West Antarctica influences sea-level rise contributions.
  • DOI: 10.1038/s41467-023-36990-3 (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-023-36990-3)

• Surawy-Stepney et al. (2023) – Episodic Dynamic Change Linked to Damage on the Thwaites Glacier Ice Tongue from 2015 to 2021. Nature Geoscience.
  • Focuses on dynamic changes in the Thwaites Glacier, a critical contributor to sea-level rise.
  • DOI: 10.1038/s41561-023-01131-4 (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41561-023-01131-4)

• Wallis et al. (2023) – Widespread seasonal speed-up of West Antarctic Peninsula glaciers from 2014 to 2021. Nature Geoscience, 16, 231–237.
  • Examines seasonal glacier speed-up in West Antarctica, a key factor in ice mass loss.
  • DOI: 10.1038/s41561-023-01131-4 (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41561-023-01131-4)

2. Coastal Sea-Level Changes
ESA EO Science Strategy Priority:
• Science Question (SQ-05): What processes drive changes in sea level in the coastal ocean?
  • Addresses ScienceTheme ST-I (Water Cycle) and ST-III (Energy Fluxes).
  • Informs Treaty PARIS (Art 4/5 Climate; Art 7 Adaptation; Art 8 Loss/Damage) and SDG 11 (Sustainable Cities), 13 (Climate Action), 14 (Life Below Water).
  • Linked to Tipping Points: Ice Sheets (TP-01), Glaciers (TP-03), and Ocean Overturning (TP-14).

items.question: What ERA5 surface variables related to precipitation and hydrology are available through the CDS API?

answers.text: The climate agent returned a comprehensive list of ERA5 surface variables related to precipitation and hydrology, along with related variables from other categories, and notes on resolution and units. I will return this result directly to the user as requested by the output rules.

Here are the ERA5 surface variables related to precipitation and hydrology available through the CDS API:

• total_precipitation: Total precipitation (liquid + solid) accumulated over the time step (m of water equivalent).
• large_scale_precipitation: Precipitation from large-scale (non-convective) processes (m of water equivalent).
• convective_precipitation: Precipitation from convective processes (m of water equivalent).
• snowfall: Snowfall accumulated over the time step (m of water equivalent).
• evaporation: Total evaporation (including transpiration) from the surface (m of water equivalent).
• potential_evaporation: Potential evaporation (evaporation that would occur under optimal conditions) (m of water equivalent).
• runoff: Total runoff (surface + subsurface) (m of water equivalent).
• surface_runoff: Surface runoff (m of water equivalent).
• sub_surface_runoff: Subsurface runoff (m of water equivalent).
• snow_evaporation: Evaporation of snow (m of water equivalent).
• snowmelt: Melted snow (m of water equivalent).
• large_scale_precipitation_fraction: Fraction of large-scale precipitation relative to total precipitation.

Here are the ERA5 surface variables related to precipitation and hydrology available through the CDS API:

Precipitation and Hydrology Variables
• total_precipitation: Total precipitation (rain, snow, etc.) in meters.
• large_scale_precipitation: Precipitation from large-scale weather systems (e.g., stratiform rain) in meters.
• convective_precipitation: Precipitation from convective processes (e.g., thunderstorms) in meters.
• snowfall: Snowfall in meters of water equivalent.
• evaporation: Evaporation from the surface in meters.
• potential_evaporation: Potential evaporation (theoretical maximum) in meters.
• runoff: Total runoff (surface + sub-surface) in meters.
• surface_runoff: Surface runoff in meters.
• sub_surface_runoff: Sub-surface runoff in meters.
• snow_evaporation: Evaporation from snow in meters.
• snowmelt: Snowmelt in meters.
• large_scale_precipitation_fraction: Fraction of large-scale precipitation (dimensionless).

Soil and Snow Variables
• volumetric_soil_water_layer_1: Soil moisture in the top layer (0–7 cm) in m³/m³.
• volumetric_soil_water_layer_2: Soil moisture in the second layer (7–28 cm) in m³/m³.
• volumetric_soil_water_layer_3: Soil moisture in the third layer (28–100 cm) in m³/m³.
• volumetric_soil_water_layer_4: Soil moisture in the fourth layer (100–289 cm) in m³/m³.
• snow_depth: Snow depth in meters.
• snow_depth_water_equivalent: Snow depth as water equivalent in meters.
• snow_cover: Fraction of grid cell covered by snow (dimensionless).
• snowmelt: Snowmelt in meters.

Moisture and Water Cycle Variables
• total_column_water_vapour: Total column water vapor in kg/m².
• total_column_rain_water: Total column rainwater in kg/m².
• total_column_snow_water: Total column snow water in kg/m².

Heat and Energy Fluxes
• surface_latent_heat_flux: Latent heat flux at the surface in J/m².
• surface_sensible_heat_flux: Sensible heat flux at the surface in J/m².

Notes
• Units: Precipitation and hydrology variables are typically provided in meters (m) for depth/flux. For example:
  • total_precipitation is in m (accumulated over the time step).
  • evaporation and runoff are also in m.
• Conversion: To convert precipitation from meters to millimeters, multiply by 1000 (e.g., 1 m = 1000 mm).
• ERA5-Land: For higher-resolution (0.1°) land-surface variables like soil moisture, use the ERA5-Land dataset via fetch_era5_land().

Here are the ERA5 surface-level variables related to precipitation and hydrology available through the CDS API:

Precipitation and Hydrology Variables
Variable Name               | Description                                                                                     | Unitstotal_precipitation           | Accumulated liquid and frozen water (rain + snow + ice) falling to the Earth's surface.            | meters (m)
large_scale_precipitation     | Precipitation due to large-scale atmospheric dynamics (e.g., frontal systems).                     | m
convective_precipitation      | Precipitation due to convective processes (e.g., thunderstorms).                                   | m
snowfall                      | Accumulated snow falling to the surface.                                                            | m of water equivalent
evaporation                   | Total evaporation (from soil, water bodies, and vegetation).                                      | m
potential_evaporation         | Maximum possible evaporation under given atmospheric conditions (if water were unlimited).         | m
runoff                        | Total runoff (surface + subsurface) into rivers and streams.                                       | m
surface_runoff                | Water flowing over the land surface (not infiltrating into the soil).                              | m
sub_surface_runoff            | Water flowing laterally beneath the soil surface (e.g., through soil layers).                      | m
snow_evaporation              | Evaporation of snow from the surface.                                                              | m
snowmelt                      | Water produced by melting snow.                                                                    | m
large_scale_precipitation_fraction | Fraction of total precipitation attributed to large-scale processes (0–1).                     | Dimensionless (ratio)
Key Notes:
1. Units:
   • Precipitation variables are accumulated over the time step (hourly/monthly) and reported in meters (m).
   • Convert to millimeters (mm) by multiplying by 1000 (e.g., 1 m = 1000 mm).

2. Time Resolution:
   • Hourly data: Values are accumulated over the hour (e.g., total_precipitation at 01:00 UTC = precipitation from 00:00–01:00 UTC).
   • Monthly data: Values are accumulated over the entire month.

3. ERA5-Land:
   • For higher-resolution (0.1°) land-specific variables (e.g., soil moisture), use the ERA5-Land dataset instead.

4. Soil Moisture:
   • Variables like volumetric_soil_water_layer_1 (topsoil moisture) are available under \"Soil And Snow\" in the full variable list.
